questions.q: Why does a spoken project walkthrough need a different structure than a written README?
options: READMEs and spoken walkthroughs should be word-for-word identical
An interviewer is listening, not reading, and can't scroll back up — the structure has to work for speech
Interviewers never ask about architecture diagrams
Spoken walkthroughs should contain less technical detail than a README
questions.explain: The four-part Situation, Design, Trade-off, Retrospect structure is built specifically for a listener who can't revisit earlier points.

questions.q: What are the four parts of the structure this lesson recommends for a project walkthrough?
options: Kickoff, Ingestion, Scoring, Wrap-up
Introduction, Body, Conclusion, Questions
Situation, Design, Trade-off, Retrospect
Problem, Code, Tests, Deployment
questions.explain: Situation covers the constraint that mattered most; Design and Trade-off cover the choice and its cost; Retrospect covers what you'd change now.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say "I built a fraud detector using Eventstreams and KQL" is a weaker interview answer than explaining the sliding-window choice?
options: Eventstreams and KQL are considered outdated technologies
It's factually incorrect about the project
It states the what, which is nearly interchangeable with any other candidate's answer, rather than the why, which only the person who made the decision can explain convincingly
Interviewers only care about programming languages, not architecture
questions.explain: The why — like choosing a sliding window specifically to avoid undercounting a fraud burst — is what differentiates a real decision-maker's answer.

questions.q: Where does the "why" behind a project's trade-offs already exist, according to this lesson?
options: It has to be invented fresh for each interview
In the honest, specific retrospectives written for each project back in Lessons 74 and 78
It doesn't exist until the interview itself
In the original project requirements documents
questions.explain: The retrospective's own questions about what worked, what you'd change, and what surprised you map directly onto the trade-off and retrospect parts of the interview structure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend rehearsing trade-off answers out loud, rather than just having them ready mentally?
options: A trade-off that's clear in your head often comes out tangled the first time you say it — the gap between understanding and explaining smoothly only closes with practice
Interviewers can tell if an answer wasn't rehearsed and penalize it
Rehearsal is only useful for behavioral questions, not technical ones
Written answers are legally required for technical interviews
questions.explain: Practicing out loud is what closes the gap between silently understanding a decision and being able to explain it smoothly under interview pressure.
